summary: Question: what is the systematic risk of trend-following hedge funds, whose returns are option-like and invisible to linear factor models? Method: model the primitive trend follower as a long lookback straddle, replicated with rolled exchange-traded straddles on 26 futures markets (1985-97), and regress a 407-fund CTA index and 163 individual funds on these PTFS returns. Conclusion: PTFS portfolios explain ~48% of CTA returns (vs ~1% for asset indices) and the payoffs in extreme equity months, so trend followers are long volatility/event risk.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: We use lookback straddles to model trend-following strategies, and show that they can explain trend-following funds’ returns better than standard asset indices.
claims.claim: Trend-following fund returns are option-like and are better explained by lookback straddle returns than by standard asset indices.
claims.testable: yes - regress CTA index on PTFS returns

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Though standard straddles lead to similar empirical results, lookback straddles are theoretically closer to the concept of trend following.
claims.claim: Standard straddles fit the data about as well, but lookback straddles are preferred because they match the trend-following concept in theory.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Our model should be useful in the design of performance benchmarks for trend-following funds.
claims.claim: The lookback-straddle model is offered as a basis for trend-following fund benchmarks.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: The near bankruptcy of Long-Term Capital Management (LTCM) in 1998 has further heightened attention on hedge fund risk.
claims.claim: Hedge funds do not disclose their activities and LTCM (1998) raised concern about their hidden risk, motivating a model of strategy risk.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Linear-factor models of investment styles using standard asset benchmarks, as in Sharpe (1992), are not designed to capture the nonlinear return features commonly found among hedge funds.
claims.claim: Hedge funds trade dynamically and produce option-like returns, so linear style regressions on asset indices miss their systematic risk and can wrongly suggest none exists.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: A remedy is in Glosten and Jagannathan (1994), where they suggested using benchmark-style indices that have embedded option-like features.
claims.claim: Glosten and Jagannathan (1994) recommend benchmarks with embedded option features; Fung and Hsieh (1997a) extracted such style factors, which still need linking to the markets traded.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: From a modeling perspective, it is useful to concentrate on a
claims.claim: Because funds dynamically mix several nonlinear strategies, studying a general hedge fund sample is of limited value; one should model a single strategy that many funds follow.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: a manager can generate positive Jensen’s alphas by selling call options on the underlying stocks of a given standard benchmark.
claims.claim: Footnote 3: regression alphas are biased under nonlinearity, e.g. selling calls creates positive Jensen alpha (Grinblatt-Titman); market timers produce option-like returns without trading options (Merton; Dybvig-Ross); Treynor-Mazuy and Henriksson-Merton add nonlinear regressors.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Empirically, Lehman and Modest (1987) found that a number of mutual funds exhibited option-like return features.
claims.claim: Footnote 3: option-like return features are found even among mutual funds (Lehman and Modest 1987).

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Also, Fung and Hsieh (1997b) showed that the returns of CTA funds have one dominant style factor.
claims.claim: CTA fund returns share one dominant style factor, interpreted as trend following, so CTA returns are the natural testbed.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: they tended to be large and positive during the best and worst performing months of the world equity markets.
claims.claim: Trend-following fund returns are uncorrelated with standard indices on average but large and positive in both the worst and best world equity months.
claims.indicator: MSCI world equity monthly return quintile
claims.direction: long trend followers as hedge for extreme equity months

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: The monthly returns of the world equity market, as proxied by the Morgan Stanley (MS) World Equity Index, are sorted into
claims.claim: Figure 1 method: sort monthly MS World Equity returns into five states (worst to best) and average the returns of an equal-weighted portfolio of the six largest trend-following funds in each state.
claims.exact_rule: sort months into 5 quantile states of MSCI World return; average fund returns per state
claims.data_needed: MSCI World monthly returns; trend-following fund returns

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: the state-dependent beta estimates tend to be positive in up markets and nega- tive in down markets.
claims.claim: Trend followers have near-zero average equity beta but positive beta in up markets and negative in down markets, a convex contingent-claim profile that implies (nonlinear) systematic risk.
claims.conditions: beta sign flips with market direction

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: betas from a standard linear-factor model can either overstate the systematic risk or understate it (as in the case of LTCM).
claims.claim: With nonlinear payoffs, linear betas can overstate or understate true systematic risk (LTCM understated).

claims.speaker: authors

claims.claim: Trading rules are proprietary, so the authors can only theorise what trend followers do rather than estimate risk directly.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Trend followers can converge onto the same “trend” for different reasons and have very different “entry and exit” points.
claims.claim: Trend followers differ in signals and entry/exit timing, so the model needs an aggregate that captures the style without individual idiosyncrasies.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: The combination of these two options is the lookback straddle, which delivers the ex post maximum payout of any trend-following strategy.
claims.claim: The primitive trend-following strategy (PTFS) is posited to pay like a lookback straddle (buy at the period low via lookback call, sell at the high via lookback put), the maximum ex post payout of any trend follower.
claims.exact_rule: PTFS payout over horizon = S_max - S_min (lookback call + lookback put)

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: trend followers should deliver returns resembling those of a portfolio of bills and lookback straddles.
claims.claim: Trend-following returns should look like T-bills plus long lookback straddles.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: In reality, trend followers often make multiple entry and exit decisions over a
claims.claim: Footnote 7: real trend followers trade in and out many times when volatility around the trend is sufficient; the single-trade model excludes this.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Rather, it is designed to capture the general characteristics of the entire family of trend-following strategies.
claims.claim: The option strategy does not replicate any specific technical rule (unlike rule-based studies such as Alexander 1961); it captures the family's general payoff.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: The convex return pattern observed in Figure 1 resembles the payout
claims.claim: The convex pattern in Figure 1 resembles a straddle payout on the underlying asset.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: which is the return of a portfolio of bills and a straddle on stocks.
claims.claim: Merton (1981): a perfect market timer earns bills plus a call (with short-sale constraints) or bills plus a straddle (without), so timing creates option-like returns.
claims.exact_rule: perfect timer return = R + max(0, Z - R) + max(0, R - Z)

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: These traders apply capi- tal resources to different markets in a dynamic fashion
claims.claim: Trend followers are opportunistic: they move capital across markets dynamically according to their own skill and technology.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: A trend is a series of asset prices that move persistently in one direction over a given time interval, where price changes exhibit posi- tive serial correlation.
claims.claim: A trend is persistent one-directional price movement with positively autocorrelated changes; trend followers try to detect such patterns and trade with them.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Consequently, the optimal payout of the PTFS is S max − S min .
claims.claim: With one trade per interval, a perfect market timer (PMTS) earns |S_end - S_start|, while a perfect trend follower (PTFS) earns S_max - S_min.
claims.exact_rule: PMTS optimal payout = |S' - S|; PTFS optimal payout = S_max - S_min (single trade per interval)

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Note that we are not advocating that markets trend.
claims.claim: Footnote 9: whether markets trend is left as an open empirical question; the paper models the payoff only.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Capital allocation to the PMTS or PTFS is determined by comparing the payout of the respective strategy to the return of the risk-free asset.
claims.claim: Capital is split between the strategy and the risk-free asset by comparing payout with the risk-free return (and investor risk preference, footnote 11).

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Generally, market timers enter into a trade in anticipa- tion of a price move over a given time period, whereas trend followers trade
claims.claim: Market timers trade on forecasts before a move; trend followers trade only after observing a price move (buying breakouts, selling breakdowns).

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Therefore, if Merton’s (1981) assumptions were strictly imposed, the payout of the PTFS must equal that of the PMTS.
claims.claim: Footnote 10: under Merton's strict assumptions (trading only at period start/end) the two strategies have the same payout.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Breakout means that the price of an asset moves above a recent high, and buying breakouts refers to the strategy of going long when a breakout happens.
claims.claim: Footnote 12: breakout = price above a recent high (go long); breakdown = price below a recent low (go short).
claims.exact_rule: long when price > recent high; short when price < recent low (lookback length unspecified)
claims.indicator: price breakout above recent high / below recent low

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: the PMTS is a long position in a standard straddle, and the PTFS is a long position in a lookback straddle.
claims.claim: Because real costs are unknown, the ex ante cost of the market timer is set to an at-the-money standard straddle premium and that of the trend follower to a lookback straddle premium.
claims.exact_rule: PMTS = long ATM straddle; PTFS = long lookback straddle; cost = option premium

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: we will empirically create returns of the PTFS using lookback straddles on 26 different markets.
claims.claim: PTFS returns are built for 26 markets.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: The delta of the standard straddle is given by
claims.claim: Under Black-Scholes the standard straddle delta is 2N(a1) - 1, while the lookback straddle delta (Goldman et al. 1979) depends on the running max M and min Q since inception.
claims.exact_rule: delta_straddle = 2N(a1) - 1; a1 = [ln(S/X) + (r + sigma^2/2)T]/(sigma sqrt(T)); lookback delta per eq (3)-(12)

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: The key difference lies in the path-dependency of the lookback option.
claims.claim: The lookback straddle differs from a standard straddle through path dependency on the running high and low.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Consequently, as the investment horizon shrinks, the payouts of the two strategies converge.
claims.claim: The two payouts are equal only when the max and min fall at the period ends, so they converge for short horizons and diverge for longer ones.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: In the empirical implementation, we use three-month options, which tend to be the most liquid options
claims.claim: Three-month options are used because they are the most liquid, although this horizon may be too short to separate lookback from standard straddles.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: The rollover process is much reminiscent of the buying breakouts and selling breakdowns characteristics of trend-following strategies.
claims.claim: A lookback straddle can be replicated by rolling standard straddles (Goldman et al. 1979), which mirrors breakout trading; because both strategies use straddles their returns are likely correlated.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: We do not attempt to answer the question of which option portfolio best describes the returns of trend- following funds.
claims.claim: The goal is only to show that one bills-plus-lookback-straddle portfolio behaves like trend followers; other option portfolios might replicate better.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: For stock indices, we used the futures contracts on the S&P 500 (CME), Nikkei 225 (Osaka), FTSE 100 (LIFFE), DAX 30 (DTB), and the Australian All Ordinary Index (SFE).
claims.claim: Universe of 26 futures markets: 5 stock indices, 5 government bonds (US 30Y, Gilt, Bund, French 10Y, Australia 10Y), 4 currencies (GBP, DEM, JPY, CHF on CME), 6 short rates (Eurodollar, Euro-DM, Euro-Yen, PIBOR, Short Sterling, Aus bank bills) and 6 commodities (soybean, wheat, corn, gold, silver, crude).
claims.exact_rule: 26 markets: S&P500, Nikkei225, FTSE100, DAX30, All Ords; US30Y, Gilt, Bund, French10Y, Aus10Y; GBP, DEM, JPY, CHF; Eurodollar, Euro-DM, Euro-Yen, PIBOR, Short Sterling, Aus BA; soybean, wheat, corn, gold, silver, crude
claims.data_needed: futures and options on the listed exchanges

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Futures data on the CBOT, CME, and NYMEX came from Datastream.
claims.claim: Data: futures and options from the Futures Industry Institute (DTB, MATIF, Osaka, CME options), the exchanges (LIFFE, SFE, TIFFE; CBOT/NYMEX options) and Datastream (CBOT, CME, NYMEX futures).
claims.data_needed: FII, LIFFE, SFE, TIFFE, CBOT, NYMEX, CME, Datastream

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: We use one strad- dle to lock in the high price of the underlying asset by rolling this straddle to a higher strike whenever the price of the underlying asset moves above the current strike.
claims.claim: Lookback straddles are replicated by buying two ATM straddles and rolling one up to the new strike at each new high and the other down at each new low, so at expiry they pay S_max - S_min.
claims.exact_rule: at inception buy 2 ATM straddles; straddle 1: roll to strike = new high whenever price > strike; straddle 2: roll to strike = new low whenever price < strike; hold to 3-month expiry
claims.data_needed: daily futures and option settlement prices across strikes

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: An alternative replication strategy is a delta-hedging strategy using the underlying asset.
claims.claim: Footnote 14: delta-hedging with the underlying was rejected because it needs an assumed implied volatility for an untraded lookback.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: In replicating this, the straddle rolls may generate additional cash
claims.claim: Roll cash flows from moving straddle strikes are included in PTFS returns, because rolling does not reproduce the lookback's two-cash-flow profile exactly.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Most of the options traded on U.S. exchanges are American-style options, which have higher prices than European-style options. This biases downward the returns of the PTFS.
claims.claim: Using American options (US exchanges) overstates the option cost, biasing PTFS returns down; LIFFE futures-style options are unaffected.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: we use the nearest-to-the- money options to approximate at-the-money options.
claims.claim: Discrete strikes mean the nearest-to-the-money options proxy ATM; the authors judge the error small.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: we used lookback straddles with three months to expiration as close to the end of a quarter as possible to maintain consistency.
claims.claim: Lookback straddles use quarterly expiries (Mar/Jun/Sep/Dec), initiated about three months before expiry near quarter end, for liquidity and comparability across markets.
claims.exact_rule: initiate 3 months to expiry near each quarter end; quarterly expirations

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: In practice, we rolled the straddles only at the end of each trading day using the settlement prices of the options and the underlying assets.
claims.claim: Rolls are done once a day at settlement prices (not continuously), and daily returns are compounded to monthly to match hedge fund reporting.
claims.exact_rule: daily roll at settlement; aggregate daily returns to monthly

claims.speaker: authors

claims.claim: Five equal-weighted PTFS portfolios are formed: stocks, bonds, three-month rates, currencies, commodities.

reasoning.question: How can investors see the systematic risk of hedge fund strategies whose returns are nonlinear, using trend-following CTAs as the case? It matters because linear factor models make such funds look riskless and uncorrelated, which misleads risk budgeting and benchmarking.

thesis.statement: A primitive trend follower has the payoff of a lookback straddle (long the realised range), so trend-following returns behave like long volatility / market-event-risk options; portfolios of lookback straddles on 26 futures markets explain about half of CTA index variance and the extreme-month payoffs, where asset-class benchmarks explain almost none.

foundations.premise: Dynamic trading strategies generate option-like (nonlinear) returns, which linear regressions on asset benchmarks miss or misstate.
CTA returns are dominated by one common style, trend following.
foundations.support: PCA in Fung-Hsieh 1997b, updated on TASS

foundations.premise: Trend followers enter after a move (breakouts) and aim to capture the range between high and low, whose ideal payoff is S_max - S_min.
The fair cost of perfect trend following equals the lookback straddle premium, observable via exchange-traded options.
Extreme market moves stem from common macro shocks that hit all financial markets together.
Whether markets actually trend is not asserted.

reasoning.forward_looking_inputs: (reader) The paper's factor is contemporaneous, so it does not itself forecast. Its logic implies trend-following P&L ~ realised range (max - min over ~3 months) in currencies, bonds/short rates and commodities minus the option-implied premium for that range. Hence the observable inputs that should lead trend-following returns over the next quarter are (a) the gap between expected realised range/volatility and option-implied volatility in FX, rates and commodities, and (b) the probability of common macro shocks that move many financial markets together. The edge fades when implied vol is rich relative to subsequent realised range, when markets are range-bound or reverse quickly within the window, or when equity tail events are not accompanied by large cross-asset moves.
reader_inferences: (reader) Because standard and lookback straddles fit equally at monthly frequency, the evidence supports 'trend followers are long volatility' more than the specific lookback mechanism.
(reader) The persistent ~1.2%/month constant suggests funds capture the range more cheaply than the option premium (or harvest a trend premium) - an untested source of return.
(reader) The 1985-97 sample includes the 1987 crash, 1990 Gulf War and a long bond rally, which favour trend followers; results may be sample-specific.
(reader) PTFS factors can be rebuilt today from listed options (or straddle approximations) to benchmark CTA allocations and to size them as crisis hedges.
